clinicalPearls: An abnormal bony, cartilaginous or fibrous union between two or more tarsal bones arising from a failure of embryonic segmentation, not an osteonecrosis or apophysitis
The two most common types are calcaneonavicular and talocalcaneal (subtalar) coalitions
Typically becomes symptomatic in later childhood or adolescence, roughly eight to sixteen years, as a fibrous or cartilaginous bar ossifies and stiffens
Presents with a rigid flatfoot, recurrent ankle sprains, activity-related hindfoot pain and limited subtalar motion
The classic clinical picture is a peroneal spastic flatfoot, in which the peroneal muscles are held in protective spasm and the hindfoot does not invert on tiptoe standing
Radiographic clues include the C-sign and talar beaking in talocalcaneal coalition and the anteater nose sign in calcaneonavicular coalition
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging confirms the coalition, defines its type and extent and detects secondary joint changes
Management ranges from activity modification, orthoses and immobilisation for symptom control to surgical resection or arthrodesis as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Tarsal coalition results from a failure of normal segmentation of the primitive mesenchyme during foetal development, so that two or more tarsal bones remain abnormally joined by bone (synostosis), cartilage (synchondrosis) or fibrous tissue (syndesmosis). Early in life a fibrous or cartilaginous coalition may permit some movement and remain asymptomatic, but as the child grows the bar tends to ossify and progressively restrict motion at the affected joint, most often the subtalar or calcaneonavicular articulation. The loss of hindfoot mobility transfers abnormal stress to adjacent joints and provokes protective spasm of the peroneal muscles, producing the characteristic rigid, everted flatfoot. Over time the restricted, abnormally loaded joints are prone to secondary degenerative change.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory or juvenile idiopathic arthritis of the hindfoot
Infection or tumour of the hindfoot
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing foot radiographs including an oblique view for calcaneonavicular coalition
Assessment for the C-sign, talar beaking and the anteater nose sign
Computed tomography to define bony coalitions and their extent
Magnetic resonance imaging to detect fibrous or cartilaginous coalitions and marrow oedema
Clinical assessment of subtalar motion and hindfoot flexibility on tiptoe standing
Examination for peroneal muscle spasm reproducing the rigid flatfoot
redFlags: A rigid, painful flatfoot that does not correct on tiptoe standing, indicating a fixed structural cause
Established secondary degenerative change in the subtalar or adjacent joints
Progressive pain and deformity limiting walking despite conservative measures
Atypical features such as warmth, swelling or systemic upset suggesting infection or inflammatory arthritis
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with conservative measures, particularly when a limited coalition is treated before secondary arthritis develops; larger coalitions, established degenerative change or persistent pain may require surgery, with resection favoured for smaller bars and arthrodesis for extensive coalitions or arthritic joints.
pitfalls: Labelling a rigid flatfoot as a simple flexible flatfoot and missing an underlying coalition
Relying on plain radiographs alone and overlooking a fibrous or cartilaginous coalition best seen on cross-sectional imaging
Attributing recurrent ankle sprains to instability without recognising restricted subtalar motion
Proceeding to resection when extensive coalition or established arthritis would be better served by arthrodesis
management: Begin with conservative management using activity modification, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesia and supportive orthoses to offload the hindfoot
Use a period of cast or walking-boot immobilisation to settle acute pain and peroneal spasm
Provide physiotherapy for hindfoot stretching, peroneal spasm and strengthening once acute symptoms settle
Consider a corticosteroid injection to the coalition for persistent inflammatory pain
Offer surgical resection of the bar with interposition of fat or muscle for smaller symptomatic coalitions without established arthritis
Reserve arthrodesis for extensive coalitions or established secondary degenerative change
Refer persistent or disabling cases to orthopaedic foot and ankle surgery
